item_verbatim: Quantum information science (QIS) exploits quantum principles to transform how information is acquired, encoded, manipulated, and applied. Quantum information science encompasses quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing, and spurs other advances in science and technology.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.3), Key Concept 1
extra: level=key concept; concept=1; group=1 (defines field); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum information science employs quantum mechanics, a well-tested theory that uses the mathematics of probability, vectors, algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, and linear transformations to describe the physical world.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 1a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=1; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum information science combines information theory and computer science, following the laws of quantum mechanics, to process information in fundamentally new ways.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 1b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=1; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum information science has already produced and enhanced high-impact technologies such as the Global Positioning System (GPS), which depends on the extreme precision of atomic clocks based on the quantum states of atoms.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 1c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=1; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: A quantum state is a mathematical representation of a physical system, such as an atom, and provides the basis for processing quantum information.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.3), Key Concept 2
extra: level=key concept; concept=2; group=2-6 (necessary ideas); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum states are represented by directions or vectors in an abstract space.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 2a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=2; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: The direction of the quantum state vector determines the probabilities of all of the possible outcomes of a set of measurements. Quantum manipulations in the physical world follow vector operations, incorporating complex numbers and negative values. This captures a behavior of physical quantum systems that cannot be described solely by the arithmetic of probability.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 2b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=2; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum systems are fragile. For instance, measurement almost always disturbs a quantum system in a way that cannot be ignored. This fragility influences the design of computational algorithms and communication and sensing protocols.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 2c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=2; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum applications are designed to carefully manipulate fragile quantum systems without observation to increase the probability that the final measurement will provide the intended result.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.3), Key Concept 3
extra: level=key concept; concept=3; group=2-6 (necessary ideas); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: A measurement is an interaction with the quantum system that transforms a state with multiple possible outcomes into a “collapsed” state that now has only one outcome: the measured outcome.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 3a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=3; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: A quantum state determines the probability of the outcome of a single quantum measurement, but one outcome rarely reveals complete information about the system.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 3b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=3; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Repeated measurements on identically prepared quantum systems are required to determine more complete information about the state.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 3c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=3; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Because of the limitations of quantum measurement (providing only partial information and disturbing the system), quantum states cannot be copied or duplicated.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 3d
extra: level=fundamental; concept=3; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: The quantum bit, or qubit, is the fundamental unit of quantum information, and is encoded in a physical system, such as polarization states of light, energy states of an atom, or spin states of an electron.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.3), Key Concept 4
extra: level=key concept; concept=4; group=2-6 (necessary ideas); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Unlike a classical bit, each qubit can represent information in a superposition, or vector sum that incorporates two mutually exclusive quantum states.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 4a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=4; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: At a particular moment in time, a set of n classical bits can exist in only one of 2n possible states, but a set of n qubits can exist in a superposition of all of these states. This capability allows quantum information to be stored and processed in ways that would be difficult or impossible to do classically.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.3, fundamental 4b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=4; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Multiple qubits can also be entangled, where the measurement outcome of one qubit is correlated with the measurement outcomes of the others.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 4c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=4; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Entanglement, an inseparable relationship between multiple qubits, is a key property of quantum systems necessary for obtaining a quantum advantage in most QIS applications.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.4), Key Concept 5
extra: level=key concept; concept=5; group=2-6 (necessary ideas); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: When multiple quantum systems in superposition are entangled, their measurement outcomes are correlated. Entanglement can cause correlations that are different from what is possible in a classical system.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 5a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=5; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: An entangled quantum system of multiple qubits cannot be described solely by specifying an individual quantum state for each qubit.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 5b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=5; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum technologies rely on entanglement in different ways. When a fragile entangled state is maintained, a computational advantage can be realized. The extreme sensitivity of entangled states, however, can enhance sensing and communication.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 5c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=5; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: For quantum information applications to be successfully completed, fragile quantum states must be preserved, or kept coherent.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.4), Key Concept 6
extra: level=key concept; concept=6; group=2-6 (necessary ideas); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Decoherence erodes superposition and entanglement through undesired interaction with the surrounding environment. Uncontrolled radiation, including light, vibration, heat, or magnetic fields, can all cause decoherence.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 6a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=6; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Some types of qubits are inherently isolated, whereas others require carefully-engineered materials to maintain their coherence.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 6b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=6; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: High decoherence rates limit the length and complexity of quantum computations; implementing methods that correct errors can mitigate this issue.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 6c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=6; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum computers, which use qubits and quantum operations, will solve certain complex computational problems more efficiently than classical computers.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.4), Key Concept 7
extra: level=key concept; concept=7; group=7-9 (areas of study); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Qubits can represent information compactly; more information can be stored and processed using 100 qubits than with the largest conceivable classical supercomputer.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 7a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=7; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum data can be kept in a superposition of exponentially many classical states during processing, giving quantum computers a significant speed advantage for certain computations such as factoring large numbers (exponential speed-up) and performing searches (quadratic speed-up). However, there is no speed advantage for many other types of computations.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 7b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=7; verbatim_check=tokens

item_verbatim: A fault-tolerant quantum computer corrects all errors that occur during quantum computation, including those arising from decoherence, but error correction requires significantly more resources than the original computation.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 7c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=7; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum communication uses entanglement or a transmission channel, such as optical fiber, to transfer quantum information between different locations.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.4), Key Concept 8
extra: level=key concept; concept=8; group=7-9 (areas of study); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum teleportation is a protocol that uses entanglement to destroy quantum information at one location and recreate it at a second site, without transferring physical qubits.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 8a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=8; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum cryptography enhances privacy based on quantum physics principles and cannot be circumvented. Due to the fragility of quantum systems, an eavesdropper’s interloping measurement will almost always be detected.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.4, fundamental 8b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=8; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum sensing uses quantum states to detect and measure physical properties with the highest precision allowed by quantum mechanics.
locator: Nine Key Concepts list p.2 (restated p.5), Key Concept 9
extra: level=key concept; concept=9; group=7-9 (areas of study); verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle describes a fundamental limit in simultaneously measuring two specific, separate attributes. “Squeezing” deliberately sacrifices the certainty of measuring one attribute in order to achieve higher precision in measuring the other attribute; for example, squeezing is used in LIGO to improve sensitivity to gravitational waves.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.5, fundamental 9a
extra: level=fundamental; concept=9; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum sensors take advantage of the fact that physical qubits are extremely sensitive to their surroundings. The same fragility that leads to rapid decoherence enables precise sensors. Examples include magnetometers, single-photon detectors, and atomic clocks for improvements in medical imaging and navigation, position, and timing.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.5, fundamental 9b
extra: level=fundamental; concept=9; verbatim_check=exact

item_verbatim: Quantum sensing has vastly improved the precision and accuracy of measurements of fundamental constants, freeing the International System of Units from its dependence on one-of-a-kind artifacts. Measurement units are now defined through these fundamental constants, like the speed of light and Planck’s constant.
locator: Key Concepts with Supporting Fundamentals p.5, fundamental 9c
extra: level=fundamental; concept=9; verbatim_check=exact
